questions.prompt: What is the size of a SHA-1 digest?
questions.explanation: SHA-1 keeps five 32-bit registers (A to E), giving a 160-bit digest that is written as 40 hexadecimal characters. MD5 is 128 bits and SHA-256 is 256 bits.

questions.prompt: What block size does SHA-1 process at a time?
questions.explanation: The compression function takes a 512-bit block (sixteen 32-bit words). SHA-512 uses 1024-bit blocks, which is why the two are often confused.

questions.prompt: How many steps does the SHA-1 compression function run per block?
questions.explanation: SHA-1 runs 80 steps, organised as four rounds of 20 steps. Each round uses its own logical function and its own constant K.

questions.prompt: Which sequence gives the SHA-1 round functions in order?
questions.explanation: Steps 0-19 use Ch, 20-39 use Parity (XOR), 40-59 use Maj (majority), and 60-79 use Parity again.

questions.prompt: Which step turns the 16 message words into 80 words in SHA-1?
options: Each new word is the sum of the previous two words
Each new word is the XOR of four earlier words rotated left by 1
Each new word is a copy of a word 16 positions earlier
Each new word is the hash of the previous block
questions.explanation: W[t] = ROTL1(W[t-3] XOR W[t-8] XOR W[t-14] XOR W[t-16]). The rotation by 1 is the key difference from the original SHA-0, which lacked it.

questions.prompt: A message is 3 bytes long. How many zero bytes are added after the 0x80 byte during padding?
questions.explanation: Before the 8-byte length field the data must be 56 bytes long (56 mod 64). The 3 message bytes plus the 0x80 byte make 4 bytes, so 52 zero bytes are needed. You can confirm this in the Padding view for the input abc.

questions.prompt: What is appended at the very end of the padded message?
options: The original message length in bits as a 64-bit big-endian integer
A checksum of the zero padding
questions.explanation: The last 8 bytes store the original length in bits, big-endian. Including the length prevents messages that differ only in trailing zeros from producing the same padded input.

questions.prompt: What does the avalanche effect require of a good hash function?
options: Changing one input bit changes about half of the output bits
Changing one input bit changes only one output bit
The output length grows with the input length
Equal inputs give different outputs each time
questions.explanation: A good hash flips about 50 percent of its output bits for any small input change. For SHA-1 that is around 80 of the 160 bits, which you can measure in the Avalanche view.

questions.prompt: What was demonstrated by the SHAttered attack in 2017?
options: A preimage attack that recovers any message from its digest
A practical collision: two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 digest
A way to reverse the padding step
A proof that SHA-1 is faster than SHA-256
questions.explanation: SHAttered produced two different files with an identical SHA-1 digest, the first practical collision. Preimage resistance was not broken, but collision resistance is no longer reliable.

questions.prompt: Which hash function is recommended instead of SHA-1 for new digital signatures?
questions.explanation: SHA-256 (SHA-2 family) or SHA-3 should be used. MD5 is also broken, CRC32 is only an error-detecting checksum, and SHA-0 was withdrawn because of a flaw.
